 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                         §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                     §
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                   §
 IN THE ERCOT REGION                          §                    OF TEXAS


                          COMMENTS OF CHEVRON U.S.A. INC.

                                         I. Introduction

Chevron Corporation (“Chevron” or “we”) submits these comments in response to the Public
Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) Staff Proposal for Publication to Update
Wholesale and IOU Retail Transmission Cost Recovery in the ERCOT Region. Chevron
appreciates the Commission Staff’s efforts to implement the directives in Senate Bill 6 and its
focus on ensuring that transmission costs are allocated in a manner consistent with cost-causation
principles.
Chevron is one of the world’s leading integrated energy companies. We believe affordable,
reliable and ever-cleaner energy is essential to enabling human progress. Chevron produces
crude oil and natural gas; manufactures transportation fuels, lubricants, petrochemicals and
additives; and develops technologies that enhance our business and the industry.

Chevron and its legacy companies have been a fixture in the Permian Basin for more than 100
years. Chevron’s large acreage position and talented workforce enable it to be one of the largest
producers of oil and natural gas in the basin. We produce on average more than one million
barrels of oil equivalent per day and utilize behind-the-meter power investments to support our
operations. These generation assets reduce Chevron’s reliance on grid-supplied power and can
free transmission capacity during peak demand periods when they are operating. As Chevron
increases its oil and gas production in the Permian Basin, we will be requiring more power to
meet the demands of our operations and are continuing to make investments to provide
electricity for our oil and gas operations.

Any changes to the cost allocation framework should consider the impact on existing on-site
customer-owned behind-the-meter power generation projects. Regulatory certainty is a
cornerstone of transmission regulation because transmission and behind-the-meter generation
investments are long-lived infrastructure assets that require significant upfront capital and are
evaluated based on the regulatory framework in place at the time investment decisions are made.
Efficient transmission investment depends upon regulatory, planning, compensation, and cost-
allocation frameworks that align costs with benefits and provide appropriate investment
 incentives for infrastructure development.1 Transmission cost-allocation methodologies therefore
play a significant role in shaping investment decisions regarding long-lived transmission and
generation assets.2 Material changes to cost-allocation rules after investments have been
committed can undermine investment-backed expectations, diminish the value of prior
investments, and discourage future capital deployment in resources that support reliability and
economic growth.

On-site customer-owned behind-the-meter investments support continued economic growth and
business expansion while providing reliability benefits to the grid. Chevron encourages the
Commission to consider grandfathering existing customer-owned behind-the-meter investments
that were developed under the current transmission cost allocation framework and prior to
passage of Senate Bill 6 (SB 6) and to consider maintaining the existing transmission cost
allocation framework for future behind-the-meter investments.
    II. Chevron Has Made Significant Long-Term Investments in Behind-the-Meter Energy
                                      Infrastructure

Chevron has made significant investments in behind-the-meter power infrastructure to serve its
oil and gas operations in the Permian Basin. Chevron’s power facilities in the Permian are
expected to soon total approximately 76 MW of generating capacity across three facilities,
representing roughly $128 million of capital investment. These resources are primarily used to
serve associated operational load while displacing energy that would otherwise be purchased
from the grid during operating periods and are expected to remain part of the Company’s power
supply portfolio for approximately 30 years.

Chevron has made significant investments in both Permian Basin oil and gas operations and the
energy infrastructure that supports those operations. Since 2015, Chevron has invested nearly
$40 billion in the Permian Basin and grown production at an average annual rate of more than
15%. Yet Chevron’s ERCOT load associated with its oil and gas operations has remained
relatively stable over that same period, reflecting operational efficiencies, portfolio optimization,
and investments in behind-the-meter power infrastructure. This demonstrates how industrial
customers can support production growth without a corresponding increase in electricity demand
from the grid.

                III. Investments Were Evaluated Under the Existing Framework

The Commission is proposing to replace the existing four-coincident peak (4CP) methodology
with a 12-coincident peak (12CP) methodology measured in 30-minute intervals. Chevron made



1
  See Hogan, William W., Transmission Benefits and Cost Allocation (May 31, 2011), Harvard Electricity Policy
Group and Joskow, Paul L. Facilitating Transmission Expansion to Support Efficient Decarbonization of the
Electricity Sector, MIT CEEPR Research Brief No. 2021-009.
2
  Id.
 investments in its behind-the-meter facilities under the existing framework, and the first of these
power facilities were placed in service prior to passage of SB 6.

The existing transmission cost allocation structures were among the factors that Chevron
considered when evaluating the long-term project economics of the power facilities and the
change from 4CP to 12CP may increase transmission cost obligations for these facilities. Under
the proposed 12CP framework, Chevron’s Texas Permian Basin projects will likely experience a
material reduction in expected benefits.

The proposal could also discourage future investment in on-site customer-owned generation
resources. The change to 12CP reduces a portion of the transmission and distribution savings
associated with on-site customer-funded power investments and may affect the economics of
future projects. As a result, some industrial customers may be less likely to invest in on-site
generation resources that help meet operational electricity needs and reduce reliance on grid-
supplied power.

  IV. Behind-the-Meter Investments Are Distinct from Traditional Curtailment Strategies
Under the existing 4CP methodology, some commercial and industrial customers can manage
transmission cost exposure by temporarily reducing load during anticipated coincident peak
intervals. This curtailment strategy generally relies on operational decisions made during a
limited number of high-demand hours each year and often requires little or no long-term capital
investment. SB 6 reflected concerns that the existing methodology encouraged customers to
modify operations in this manner, potentially inappropriately assigning transmission investment
costs.
Chevron recognizes the Commission’s interest in addressing these concerns, however, Chevron’s
reduction in 4CP demand was not achieved through operational curtailment. Instead, significant
capital was invested in behind-the-meter generation resources that supplied electricity to our
operations during those same intervals, thus reducing demand from the grid.
While both curtailment and behind-the-meter generation can reduce a customer’s contribution to
coincident peak demand, the underlying investment considerations are fundamentally different.
Curtailment is an operational strategy used during limited periods of the year, whereas behind-
the-meter generation requires substantial upfront capital investment and provides electricity to
support operations on an ongoing basis. Chevron’s facilities reduce the amount of electricity that
must be supplied from the grid during peak demand periods while helping meet growing energy
needs in the Permian. As a result, behind-the-meter investments provide benefits beyond peak-
demand management such as system stability and ancillary services, which distinguish these
facilities from strategies focused solely on curtailment.
Without any additional changes, the proposal may treat long-term capital investments in
customer-owned behind-the-meter generation similarly to strategies that achieved transmission
cost reductions through temporary curtailment. The Commission should consider whether
 customers that invest in on-site generation under the existing framework warrant different
treatment than customers whose reductions in coincident peak demand were achieved primarily
through operational load management. Where significant transmission charges are imposed on
behind-the-meter generators, self-supply will become less economic than full grid services
which, in turn, may lead to parties securing their power from the grid as opposed to their own
behind-the-meter generation.

                                      V. Recommendations

Chevron respectfully urges the Commission to grandfather existing customer-owned on-site
behind-the-meter resources that were developed under the existing transmission cost allocation
framework and consider maintaining the existing transmission cost allocation framework for
future behind-the-meter investments.

If the Commission determines that a transition to a 12CP methodology is warranted, it should
employ a weighted coincident peak approach that places greater emphasis on the months that
drive transmission planning and system investment rather than assigning equal weight to all
twelve-monthly peaks. For example, the traditional summer months should have a much higher
weighting than the shoulder months, since they still correlate to peak system demand and
therefore should dictate transmission investment. Arguably, one or two winter months could also
have a higher weighting, as winter peaks increasingly approach summer peak levels.

                                         VI. Conclusion

These recommendations support the Commission’s goal of ensuring that transmission costs are
allocated in a manner that better reflects system usage and cost causation while avoiding undue
disruption to customers that have made substantial long-term investments in behind-the-meter
generation under the existing framework. They would also help avoid unintended consequences
for future customer-funded investments that provide electricity for industrial operations, support
economic growth, and reduce reliance on grid-supplied power. Chevron appreciates the
Commission’s consideration of these comments and looks forward to continued engagement on
this important issue.

                                                     Respectfully submitted,




                                                     John Martini
                                                     General Manager
                                                     Policy & State Government Affairs
                                                     Chevron U.S.A, Inc.

                                                     Austin, TX 78701
